list.listitem: Trigeminal neuralgia (TN) is diagnosed clinically on the basis of recurrent attacks of unilateral severe facial pain; it can by primary/idiopathic which is caused by neurovascular contact with the nerve, or secondary TN. C
Order MRI with 3 high-resolution serquences to rule out secondary TN caused by mass, or demyelinating disease in selected patients.B
Carbamazepine or oxcarbazepine are the first line of treatment. B Additional medications can be added if needed, selected according to each individual case.C
Patients with primary or idiopathic TN should consider microvascular decompression, with ablation preferred for those with secondary TN.B

background.definition: Trigeminal neuralgia is a painful facial condition characterized by sudden, usually unilateral, severe, brief, stabbing, or lancinating pain that occurs in recurrent episodes involving the distribution of one or more branches of the fifth cranial (trigeminal) nerve.

list.listitem: Four to 13 new cases in 1000 people per year.
Incidence increases with age; most cases occur in patients older than 50 years.
Male to female ratio is 1:1.7.
Onset at a young age raises concerns about multiple sclerosis or tumors.

The spontaneous form of trigeminal neuralgia is believed to be caused by compression of the trigeminal nerve root at its entry into the pons (the root entry zone). The compression is caused by aberrant loop of an artery or vein in 80% to 90% of cases. Compression can also be caused by acoustic neuroma, meningioma, epidermoid or other cyst, or rarely a saccular aneurysm or arteriovenous malformation.
Demyelinating plaques at the root entry zone can cause trigeminal neuralgia, as in multiple sclerosis.
Postherpetic pain can complicate cutaneous herpes zoster outbreak in the trigeminal distribution.
Trigeminal neuropathic pain can result from unintentional injury to the trigeminal nerve from trauma or surgery.

Trigeminal deafferentiation pain can result from intentional injury to the nerve by peripheral nerve ablation, gangliolysis, or rhizotomy in an attempt to treat either trigeminal neuralgia or other related facial pain.
Trigeminal neuropathic pain and deafferentiation pain more commonly manifest as constant pain.
There may be an association with Sjogren syndrome, mixed connective tissue disorder, and systemic sclerosis.
Some studies showed that hypertension may be a risk factor for the development of trigeminal neuralgia.
The pathophysiology is not entirely clear. Compression leads to focal demyelination, which is thought to set up ectopic impulse generation, possibly causing ephaptic transmission.
Ephaptic cross-talk between different fiber types carrying facial sensations can explain how touching trigger points on the face can precipitate pain attacks.
The diagnosis is made clinically based on characteristic recurrent attacks of unilateral facial pain. C
Order MRI with 3 high-resolution serquences to rule out secondary TN caused by mass, or demyelinating disease in selected patients.B

Differential.Differential_Features: Periocular pain, tearing, conjuctival injection, ipsilateral Horner's syndrome
Pain is persistent rather than intermittent, and there are no autonomic signs or symptoms

list.listitem: The International Classification of Headache Disorders (ICHD-3) diagnostic criteria for classic trigeminal neuralgia are as follows: At least three attacks of unilateral facial pain fulfilling criteria 2 and 3. Occurring in one or more divisions of the trigeminal nerve, with no radiation beyond the trigeminal distribution. Pain has at least three of the following four characteristics: (1) Recurring in paroxysmal attacks lasting from a fraction of a second to two minutes; (2) Severe intensity; (3) Electric shock-like, shooting, stabbing or sharp in quality; (4) At least three attacks precipitated by innocuous stimuli to the affected side of the face. (Some attacks may be, or appear to be, spontaneous.) No clinically evident neurologic deficit. Not better accounted for by another ICHD-3 diagnosis. Paroxysmal attacks of pain lasting from a fraction of a second to 2 minutes, affecting one or more of the divisions of the trigeminal nerve.

Classification: The 2019 guidelines from the European Academy of Neurology point out the importance of differentiating between primary TN (which consituate both idiopathic cases and those related to vascular compression) and secondary trigeminal neurapathy related to other causes such as tumors, MS, postherpetic, and others.

Trigeminal neuralgia typically presents as sudden, severe, brief facial pain described as "electric shock" or "stabbing." The pain lasts for several seconds but tends to occur repeatedly over a period of days to weeks followed by longer pain-free intervals.
Some patients may have coexisting continuous dull pain. Occasionally trigeminal neuralgia can present as constant pain, which sometimes is referred to as trigeminal neuralgia type 2.

Trigeminal neuralgia is unilateral; the pain rarely can be bilateral but does not involve both sides simultaneously. It typically affects the distribution of V2 and/or V3 and less likely V1 (which is more commonly affected by postherpetic neuralgia). Pain can extend to involve other divisions over the long term.

The pain attacks can be triggered by chewing, smiling, talking, cold air, brushing teeth, and/or grimacing. Trigger zones in the distribution of the affected nerve may be present; lightly touching these areas often triggers an attack, commonly followed by a refractory period of several minutes during which a paroxysm cannot be provoked. Associated facial muscle spasms known as tic douloureux can be present.
The examination should show no clinically evident neurologic deficit unless a secondary cause (eg, tumor, multiple sclerosis) is present.

Brain MRI and MRA can identify underlying vascular anomaly or ectatic vessel, and more important, possible mass or demyelinating lesion. The 2019 European Academy of Neurology guidelines recommend MRI with a combination of 3 high resolution sequences be obtained for all patients to rule out secondary causes. However, the yield is low. Even at a tertiary referral center, the yield of routine MRI imaging of all patients was only 10% to 18%.

A systematic review of 13 high-quality studies with 1084 patients concluded that 3D time-of-flight MRA was highly sensitive (95%) and moderately specific (77%), with pooled positive and negative likelihood ratio of 2.72 and 0.08. Thus, a normal study is very helpful at ruling on TN.

Other tests include trigeminal reflex testing and trigeminal evoked potentials. Based on high sensitivity and specificity, AAN/EFNS guidelines concluded that an abnormal trigeminal blink reflexe is associated with increased risk of painful trigeminal neuropathy; but trigeminal evoked potentials were not considered clinically useful in making that distinction.
Suspect trigeminal neuralgia in patients presenting with unilateral intermittent lancinating facial pain that can be triggered by certain maneuvers.

Imaging to rule out mass or vascular lesions is recommended for patients who have sensory loss, are younger than 40 years, have bilateral symptoms, are refractory to conservative therapy, or have signs of other cranial nerve involvement.
Initial therapy for most patients is carbamazepine.
Initial therapy for most patients is carbamazepine (maximum dose = 1200 mg/day) or oxcarbazepine based on 2019 European guidelines.A

If pain relief is not sufficient with carbamazepine or oxcarbazepine, lamotrigine, gabapentin, botulinum toxin type A, pregabalin, baclofen or phenytoin may be added, though little research has been conducted that shows any benefit of one over another.C
If medical therapy fails or is not tolerated, consider surgical interventions, selected based on age, pain level, and comorbidities. B
Microvascular decompression is invasive, but has rare complications. It provides the best long-term relief and should be considered for the patient with primary or idiopathic trigeminal neuralgia.B
Consider ablative procedures (radiofrequency rhizotomy, glycerol rhizotomy, and gamma knife) for patients with secondary TN due to pathology other than neurovascular contact.B

For acute exacerbations, 2019 European guidelines recommend IV infusion of fosphenytoin or lidocaine. The same guidelines recommend carbamazepine or oxcarbazepine as first line drugs for long term treatment of TN. Second line or add-on therapies can include lamotrigine, gabapentin, botulinum toxin type A, pregabalin, baclofen and phenytoin.

Carbamazepine is considered the first line of treatment. It results in significant pain relief in 70% of patients in controlled trials; 2 systematic reviews found an NNT of <2. Start with low-dose carbamazepine (200 mg) 3 times per day and increase gradually (maximum dose = 1200 mg/day) to minimize side effects, such as drowsiness, dizziness, and ataxia. Monitor for neutropenia and liver toxicity. Oxcarbamazepine (Trileptal) is similarly effective.

Other antiepileptics that have been proposed for the treatment of trigeminal neuralgia include phenytoin, lamotrigine, topiramate, gabapentin, and clonazepam. However, there is insufficient evidence to support their effectiveness. They can also be added to carbamazepine if carbamazepine alone was not effective.
Lamotrigine is effective when added to carbamazepine in patients who do not respond to carbamazepine alone.
A single small study showed that pimozide reduced the pain in patients with trigeminal neuralgia refractory to carbamazepine.
Given the lack of comparative studies, selecting the second-line medication is usually made on an individual basis.

Although nonepileptic drugs such as tizanidine, baclofen, pregabalin, and tocainide have been used, there are either no RCTs or only single small RCTs or open label studies to support their use in trigeminal neuralgia. Antidepressants are effective for neuropathic pain, but studies in trigeminal neuralgia specifically are lacking.
IV therapy with phenytoin (15 mg/kg), phosphenytoin, or lidocaine (or, alternatively, opiates) can be used to treat acute exacerbations or can be used while oral medications are being titrated.

In an RCT, subcutaneous sumatriptan produced prompt analgesia without serious adverse reactions in patients with trigeminal neuralgia refractory to previous treatment. The effect persisted for a median of 7.9 hours.
Opiates can be used in combination with other drugs in more severe cases, but tolerance and addiction are possible, as well as other adverse effects.

Botulinium toxin injections in the painful areas has been evaluated against placebo in 2 randomized trials and was found to be more effective in reducing the severity of pain and frequency of attacks in medically refractory TN based on 2014 literature review. However there were concerns about the quality of the trials and small patients numbers.
Few studies have been conducted in the elderly; a review concluded that evidence-based recommendations are not possible for this group.
A systematic review 30 RCTs and 14 cohort studies found some improvement in pain from skeletal muscle relaxants, although the strength of evidence is low.

The 2019 European guidelines recommend microvascular decompression as the first-line surgical therapy for patients with primary or idiopathic TN, although neuroablative treatments are also an option. For secondary TN, neuroablative treatments are recommended when no neurovascular contact is seen on MRI.
Surgery is an option for patients who fail or do not tolerate medical treatment (~30%). Procedures are described below:

Microvascular decompression: This involves the removal or separation of various vascular structures from the trigeminal nerve. It is invasive but associated with the best long-term outcome (70% pain free in 10 years) and should be considered for young patients. Stroke (0.1%), deafness (1%), and death (0.2%) are rare complications. Typical trigeminal neuralgia can be cured by microvascular decompression more often (80%) than can trigeminal neuralgia associated with non-neuralgic interparoxysmal pain (56%).

Percutaneous radiofrequency rhizotomy: This procedures creates a lesion in the Gasserian ganglion of the trigeminal nerve through foramen ovale by the application of heat (also called radiofrequency thermocoagulation). It is less invasive than microvascular decompression, and has a higher initial success rate, but a recurrence rate of 25% to 50% within 2 to 3 years. Facial numbness and dysesthesia are also more common (25%). The technique is evolving, with studies comparing different temperatures and continuous vs pulsed application.

Glycerol rhizolysis: Rhizolysis involves the injection of glycerol into the trigeminal cistern. A tingling or burning sensation is felt on the face, and pain relief is usually immediate; therefore, it should be considered for patients with disabling pain. Sensory loss can occur and is actually associated with better long-term relief. Pain recurrence is more common (92% after 6 years).

Balloon compression: In this procedure, the gasserian ganglion is compressed using a balloon catheter inflated with 1.0 mL contrast dye for a few minutes. This produces immediate pain relief but persistent dysesthesias are common. A small RCT with 33 patients found no difference in outcomes between balloon compression and radiofrequency.

Gamma knife radiosurgery: It uses focused gamma radiation through a stereotactic frame and MRI to produce lesions at the proximal trigeminal root. It is safe and effective, with a lower incidence of facial numbness and dysesthesias (10%) than glycerol rhizolysis but pain relief takes a month or two. Recurrence is common (50% in 3 years), but may respond to repeated treatment. It is an option for patients who fail to respond to microvascular decompression. Predictors of a poor outcome following gamma knife radiosurgery include absence of neurovascular contact, hyperglycemia, failure to respond to carbamazepine, and atypical pain.
Linear accelerator radiosurgery uses another source of radiation and can be done in the outpatient setting without sedation. Pain relief also takes as long as 6 weeks.

Peripheral neurectomy: This can be performed on the suspected painful branch(es) of the trigeminal nerve—supraorbital, infraorbital, alveolar, and lingual nerves—using incision, alcohol injection, radiofrequency lesioning, or cryotherapy. There are no long-term longitudinal studies for these procedures.
Implantable peripheral nerve stimulation: a systematic review of 13 case series with 223 patients found reported benefits but no comparison groups or randomized trials.
There are no long-term prospective studies of the natural history of trigeminal neuralgia. Typically, the illness tends to wax and wane in severity and frequency of pain exacerbations. C
Occasionally, there are reported spontaneous permanent remissions of trigeminal neuralgia. C
Periodic attempts to gradually withdraw medications can be attempted in patients who remain pain free and stable for prolonged period on medical treatment.C

A review concluded that there was little research on medical management of trigeminal neuralgia in the elderly, that adverse effects were likely to be common, and that evidence-based recommendations were not possible.
